Martha and Mary

An Evergreen Catholic Gospel Reflection · Luke 10:38–42
Journey Through the Reflection

What happens here?

Jesus enters a village and is welcomed into the home of Martha. While Martha busies herself with serving, her sister Mary sits at the Lord’s feet and listens to him.

Martha becomes frustrated and asks Jesus to tell Mary to help her. Instead, Jesus gently corrects Martha: she is anxious and troubled about many things, while Mary has chosen the better part.

This scene is memorable because it is both deeply spiritual and very human. Martha’s service is real and generous. But her service has become mixed with agitation, distraction, and resentment.

The journey begins here

This reflection follows Martha and Mary through a six-scene cinematic Bible story. View the biblical reflection, read the Gospel, consider its Catholic meaning, listen to a voice from the Tradition, and end with reflection and prayer.

Biblical Reflection

Luke 10:38–42

Martha welcomes Jesus. Mary listens at his feet. As Martha grows anxious about serving, Jesus invites her to rediscover the one thing necessary: attention to him.

Follow Martha and Mary from generous welcome through anxious service to the peace that comes from listening to Christ.

The lesson behind the image

Service is good. Listening to Jesus gives that service its proper center.

The Sacred Passage

Luke 10:38–42

Martha welcomes Jesus and becomes burdened by many tasks. Mary sits at his feet and listens. Jesus gently calls Martha away from anxiety and praises Mary’s attentive choice.

Luke 10:38–42

As they went on their way, Jesus entered a village, and a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house.

She had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to his word.

But Martha was busy with much serving. She came to him and said: “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me.”

The Lord answered her: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things. One thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better part, and it shall not be taken from her.”

One detail to notice

Mary sits at the Lord’s feet. This is the posture of a disciple receiving the teaching of a master. She is not merely avoiding work; she is listening as a disciple.

← Back to the Story Continue to the Catholic Point →

The Catholic Point

Service ordered by attention to Christ

This passage is not a rejection of work, service, or hospitality. Martha is doing something good. The problem is not that she serves, but that her service has become anxious and resentful.

Jesus teaches that the Christian life begins by receiving from him before trying to do things for him. Prayer, listening, and closeness to Christ are not laziness. They are the source from which faithful service should flow.

Do not let good work crowd out attention to Christ.

Mary chooses the better part because she first receives the Lord. Martha’s service is valuable, but it must be ordered by peace, love, and attentiveness to Jesus.

← Back to the Passage Continue to Catholic Tradition →

A Voice from the Catholic Tradition

St. Augustine

St. Augustine insists that Martha did not choose a bad part. Her hospitality and service were genuinely good. Mary’s part was called better because she was already receiving from the Lord himself.

Augustine expresses the contrast beautifully: Martha was preparing food for Jesus, while Mary was being fed by Jesus through his word.

This is the golden nugget: Christian service is good, but it must remain rooted in receiving Christ. We cannot give spiritually what we have refused to receive.

Martha teaches us to serve. Mary teaches us to listen. Jesus teaches us that listening to him gives service its proper order and peace.

Martha was preparing a meal for the Lord; Mary was allowing the Lord to feed her.

For Reflection

Listen · Serve · Remain close to Christ
  1. Do I sometimes become so busy that I stop listening to Christ?
  2. When I serve others, do I do so with peace, or with anxiety and resentment?
  3. What would it mean for me this week to choose the better part?

Closing Prayer

Lord Jesus, teach me to welcome you as Martha did and to listen to you as Mary did.

Free me from anxiety, distraction, and resentful service.

Help me to choose the better part by staying close to you, so that my work may flow from peace and love.

Amen.
